#8652. Americans Bag Major First Ascent in Pakistan

Americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long new route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m). This time, Grant Stewart joined them for this off-season climb in the Karakoram.

This first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5. The climbers had to overcome several obstacles before even setting foot on the face. Like many other alpine-style teams this season, they were originally planning to climb another peak. But instead of adapting because of washed-out trails, they had bureaucratic issues. Their permit, obtained 10 months earlier, was revoked some weeks before their departure. They had to quickly find a different goal.

Meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare. Somehow, the outfitter sent it to base camp some days later. Then, Steadman had to overcome serious Acute Mountain Sickness in base camp. Their acclimatization was hampered by freak spells of bad weather. Finally, the line on Sosbun Brakk they initially chose was too hard and risky because of a hanging serac they only spotted after they began.

The team’s lonely base camp. Photo: Dane Steadman

“Back at BC, it was time to rest, regroup, and contemplate a totally different line that we’d seen from on the wall, which gave us new hope,” Steadman recalled.

Off to the north face. Photo: Dane Steadman

On October 1, the three climbers set off on that potential new line. “Instead of angling left up hard mixed ground above the cone as before, we made an arcing traverse right, across an ice apron, to gain runnels on the right side of the face,” Steadman explained.

The team gained 800m on that first day and set their first bivouac on a snowy arete, just in time to be slammed by a violent storm that kept them in their tent the whole next day.

Steep mixed terrain. Photo: Dane Steadman

A tarp to protect the team’s bivouac from falling spindrift. Photo: Dane Steadman

“In the morning, we made a gamble for the top by leaving the tent and starting up a massive gully system,” Steward wrote. “At its top, we reached another dead end in a huge serac barrier. To escape this, Dane committed to a visionary pitch, casting off up a blank slab to eventually reach an ice smear.”

Chaotic, difficult rocky sections. Photo: Dane Steadman

“A huge serac to our right and smooth slabs out left posed a serious question; eight meters of sideways teetering on tiny gneissic edges and a miraculous rock thread were the answer,” said Steadman.

“We continued up the massive hanging glacier to reach the hallucinatory final headwall of steep ice/mixed climbing and mushroom-weaving lunacy,” Stewart continued. “One final traverse with 1,800m of exposure under our feet and a magically appearing, dead-vertical ice tongue led us to the summit ridge.”

A totally vertical section. Photo: Grant Stewart

“The wild terrain on the upper mountain took longer than we wanted,” Steadman admitted. By the time they finally reached the summit, it was 4 pm, the storm was coming the following day, and they still had a long way (and many rappels) down.

Summit picture on Sosbun Brakk. Left to right, Dane Steadman, Grant Stewart, and Cody Wrincker. Photo: Dane Steadman

“The sun would set around 6 pm, so we threaded the first of 35 rappels and started down. Long after dark, we finally arrived back at our bivy ledge at around 5,800m,” Steadman recalled.

The storm was not supposed to start until noon the following day, but it was already snowing at 8 am, with still 1,200 vertical meters of descent to go.

Rappelling down the route. Photo: Dane Steadman

“Before long, we were caught in a proper storm,” Stewart explained. “We committed to a faster and hopefully safer descent by rappelling down the west rib to the Sokha/Sosbun col. By the time we reached the col, we could barely communicate over the screaming southwest wind.”

After some scary rappels in high winds down the serac band, the climbers finally reached a sheltered section of the face. They still had to deal with heavy spindrift coming from above until finally, at around 4 pm, they touched down on the glacier. And yet, the adventure was not over — especially for Grant Stewart:

Following Dane, I took maybe 10 steps when I felt the ground under me crack. Instinctively, I jumped and landed on my stomach as a huge crevasse swallowed the ground behind me. Soaking wet, we began postholing into the wan light of a mesmerizing white out.

[We stuck] to the center of the glacier as avalanches rumbled down all around in the whirling snow. After a strange eternity, the ragged colors of a tent appeared and we were greeted by ecstatic dancing, big hugs, and endless cups of chai from (our BC crew) Ibrahim and Idrees.

Happy climbers and base camp crew after a safe return from the summit. Photo: Dane Steadman

The team didn’t report their success and the details of the climb until they returned home. And then, the first words of appraisal were not for the route itself, but for the mountains and people of Gilgit-Baltistan.

“It’s a unique place…where continents and cultures collide. Trips there, while often difficult, are rewarding in ways hard to describe simply,” Steadman said. This was his third trip to the Karakoram, a place he has fallen in love with.

#8649. Yosemite At Last! — John Muir Trail Day 21

It was a fitful, fretful night.  It continued to rain for a while, off and on, and the wind came up again, continuing throughout the night.  The whole time I was worrying about staying warm, staying dry, and making the fewest possible excursions outside to pee.

On one of those, in the middle of the night, I did something clever.  I picked up my poncho, which was just lying on the ground soaking wet, and I draped it over a pine tree, so it looked like a scarecrow.  Or maybe a scare-bear?

Above all, I worried about what I would be facing in the morning.

Indeed, the morning came.  I got up reasonably early, at 6:30, and had breakfast in my tent.  In my warm, now semi-dry tent.

The good thing was that the rain had stopped.  The poncho I stood up as a decoy in the night, was now wind dried.  So, I used it for staging.  I put it on the wet ground and pulled all of my stuff out of the tent and placed it on the dry poncho.  If things were dry, they stayed dry; if wet, at least they didn’t get any wetter.

Things looked a LOT better at my camp site in the morning!

This mattered, because I had a lot of wet stuff.  I had a wet hoodie.  I had wet shorts, wet socks, and wet shoes.

After evacuating the tent, I took it down.  Thanks to the wind, the fly – that had been soaking wet — was basically dry.  But the ground cloth and the bottom of the tent were very wet.

What to do?  I could either dry them and be done with it, or pack them wet, and dry them later.  While thinking about this, I put them on logs, and laid them out to dry, so that my indecision became a decision.  When the sun peeked out a little, I put them on rocks.  Yes, it ate up a lot of time, but when they were finally dry, I could stop worrying about that issue and just hike.

At 9:00 a.m. I set off.  I was wearing wet-cold shoes, wet-cold shorts, wet-cold gloves, a wet-cold hoodie, and a wet-cold hat.  Only one thing was not wet and cold:  I decided to go ahead and use my dry socks.  I hoped that my shoes were just moist and not soaking wet, and my dry socks would be a barrier to that moisture.  That plan worked out pretty well.

Because it was cold in the aftermath of the storm, I started with a lot of energy, to get my blood flowing.  I needed it too, for the trail sang one refrain:  up, up, up, and up.

Looking back at the hill I climbed — but at least I was warm, and getting dry!

By the time I reached the ridge, and looked down on Garnet Lake, I was mostly dry and all warmed up.  Then I got lost.

I could see Garnet Lake, I just couldn’t see how to GET there!

I knew I had to go east, and I spotted a little trail to the east, so I started down that trail until it kind of disappeared.  Then I spent about ten minutes wandering around up there, trying to find my way, unable to believe the east-going trail was a false trail.  Finally, I retraced my steps far enough to notice a separate west-going trail.  That was counterintuitive, but it was the correct trail, because it eventually looped around, lower down, and went east, as I knew it should.

I name this “One Pine Tree Island” in Garnet Lake

Walking along the shore of Garnet Lake I envisioned what might have happened if I had made it to this destination in the storm the day before.  I could imagine myself, struggling with my tent in the rain, and having a huge gust of wind lift the tent like a beach ball and deposit it in the middle of the lake!  It would have been bad!  Yes, hilarious, but bad.

To reinforce the power of the storm the day before, this was Ninja Queen’s  description of her experience, as she sent it to me via text, with almost no editing:

“…you can imagine how horribly wrong the day of the storm went for me.  I should have hunkered down early like most other hikers had, but I foolishly trusted my (Garmin) InReach weather forecast a little too much, went over Island Pass (a tiny pass but a pass nonetheless) when the storm hit full force two hours early.  It was bad.  Really, really bad.  The trail flooded very quickly, got washed out and started diverging in multiple directions from the torrential downpour.  They were ankle-deep and I kept losing the actual trail; it had become mini rivers at that point.  Needless to say, I got wetted out through and through, shivering intensely, my hands no longer functioning, unable to take another step.  I ended up setting up camp on some random flat-ish spot over some vegetation that also started pooling water.  I was so afraid my tent was going to get flooded.  Almost everything inside the tent was wet and muddy as well, though I was able to change into dry sleep clothes and sleeping bag, thanks to my nylofume pack liners.  It took me a couple of hours, but I eventually warmed up in the bag, cooked and ate food inside (bears were the last of my worries at this point) and drank as little water as possible so I wouldn’t have to go out until the next morning.  Putting back on cold, dripping wet clothes the next morning felt torture-adjacent; something I hope I’ll never have to go through again.”

“It gave me a small chuckle seeing other hikers also emerge from non-established tent sites the next morning.  I quickly learned what I went through was not a typical rainstorm experience.  Almost everyone I talked to said it had been one of the worst storms they’ve seen on trail.  One guy, a firefighter, told me this was far worse than the hurricane weather he had caught on the AT (Appalachian Trail) a few years back.  Now I felt like a survivor, instead of feeling like a fair weather backpacker who crumbled at the slightest hint of bad weather.”

I filled up my water at the bridge where a stream exits the lake.  There were a lot of folks around there, laying out their tents to dry from the storm.  It was surprising, and a little disturbing, to see how much foam, and even spume-like foam, was on Garnet Lake, which looks otherwise pristine.  I didn’t ask anybody about it at the time, who would I ask?

But later I Googled AI and discovered:  “…foam usually forms naturally when decaying plants, algae, and organic debris release compounds that lower water surface tension, and wind or wave action whips air into bubbles.”  In other words, the wind from the storm had produced the foam, not some giant industrial complex just out of view!

I continued up, from Garnet to beautiful Ruby Lake, then to Emerald Lake, and finally the Thousand Islands Lake.  This was an exceptionally scenic stretch.

I think this was Ruby Lake… if the water were sparkling red, it would be easier to tell!

Of course this was Thousand Islands Lake — with a pretty terrific backdrop!

There was very little elevation gain from there to Island Pass.  Once the trail reached the ridge on the opposite side of the lake it seemed to stay at a mostly constant elevation for a very long time.  The longer it went on, the more I wondered, “Pass?  Is there really a pass up here somewhere?  Where?”

No pass, but a pretty cool-looking mushroom!

How can you tell when you have reached a pass?  When you can see the other side of the mountain.  It felt like that was never going to happen.

Finally, it was getting to be lunchtime.  I decided to sit next to a charming little pond up there, and to eat my lunch.

Basically, I ate half of the food that I had brought as lunch, saving the other half for “second lunch.”  But afterwards, I just didn’t feel like I had much energy.  Even finally reaching the edge did not inspire me.  I saw the edge of the pass and started heading down, but my legs felt heavy.  My legs felt like limp spaghetti.

When your legs don’t want to go, you need your brain to execute an override.  So, I forced myself to keep going.  Finally, I stopped again and made myself a second lunch in that sort of halfway space between Island Pass and Donohue Pass.  About five miles separated them and Donohue represented the entrance to Yosemite National Park.

A dead tree by a stream; dead is how I felt before second lunch!

After lunch I had more energy, and I continued.

Throughout the JMT, whenever I approached a location where I knew there was a pass in the ridgeline, I always looked up to see if I could figure out where it might be.  “Is that it?  No, is that it?  Wait, is that it?”  I suspect most hikers do this.

With Donohue Pass it was hidden around the corner of an extending hump of rock, so of course I guessed wrong.  Just short of the summit, I saw a full backpack about 25 yards from the trail.  That seemed strange and I looked around.  Was someone off going to the bathroom?  There was nothing but silence.  I continued on, but with a nagging worry for whoever was not connected with their pack.

When I arrived on top, at 11,066 feet elevation, I was all alone.  In honor of my son Gabriel, who coined the pun, I bellowed, “YO!  SEMITE!!!”  I got no answer, not even an echo.  Even so, I was in Yosemite.  It felt strange to be just a few days from the end — barring injury, of course.

As I headed down from Donohue, I thought, “On the one hand, I don’t want to set up in the dark.  But there are not too many campsites up here and, of course, I am a couple of miles behind schedule because of the storm.”  I resolved to take a chance and push it a little bit.

As a result, the riverside campsites just below Donohue Pass did not tempt me; they were filling up in any case.

The first camp north of Donohue Pass was by this ugly little lake…

Instead, I descended rapidly and with determination.  As I did, I encountered a group heading southbound, up to the pass behind me.  One young man was not carrying a pack.  Apparently, he had come down to assist his family in making the ascent.  He told me, “I left my pack up near the Pass so that I would not be encumbered in helping my family.”  I breathed deeply; mystery solved.

The first stretch went through rocky scree.  I asked the mountain gods, “Why is there so much rocky scree?”  They rewarded me with forest.

See the meadow, far below there? My campsite was somewhere down there…

The descent continued sharply through the woods, and I passed several gorgeous camping sites near the steeply dropping steam.  Each time I told myself, “No!  Not yet!” and then each time I regretted it, and wondered if I would ever find another spot, after that perfect one I had just rejected.

At last, the steep downhill tapered off, and I reached the valley at the bottom.  The stream, now wider and larger, and the trail continued to parallel each other.  The going became easier for both the water and my legs.

Following the river there were a few more possible places.  As the sun slipped behind the mountains, but still with plenty of light, I saw a knoll overlooking a wide meadow.  On that knoll was a lovely camping spot.  I was home for the night.

The sun remains on the hillside, even as it gets dark in the valley

My dinner was rice and beans and chicken, Santa Fe style.  I let it soak as I pitched my tent and arranged my site.  I let it soak some more as I explored higher up, in the giant granite boulders above the site, to find a cat hole location.  It soaked still longer as I dug the hole in preparation for the next morning.  But then, with no chores left to do, I got impatient.  I ate.

The dish was very well-seasoned, very tasty.  This was certainly a meal I would recommend having again, on another hike, in another place.  But rice takes a long time to absorb water when cold-soaking, and I didn’t wait long enough.   The flavors were great, but the rice was… crunchy.   I didn’t care much.  It had been a strenuous day, coming the day after the intense storm.  I was tired and hungry and starved for calories.  I ate it all with gusto, crunch and all!

I was feeling good.  It was a long day, and I had crossed two passes.  I was finally in Yosemite.  I haven’t mentioned the aftermath of my fall too much in recent posts, but my ribs were finally hurting less.  My wrist was still a problem, to some degree, but it was functional.

The next day, I would be passing through Tuolumne Meadow.  There I would either get a permit for Half Dome, or I would not.  If I did, I probably had three days of hiking left.  If I did not, then it would likely be two days.  I had well under forty miles to go.

As the twilight deepened, I was loving my campsite facing the open meadow.  I was proud of the mileage I had achieved, after the shortened day in the storm.  My eyes closed and I welcomed blissful sleep.

#8647. Weekend Warm-Up: Assynt

Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.

The croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries. Crofters lived on their crofts and farmed for subsistence, grazing sheep on shared land. Unable to support themselves on the croft alone, most also worked in fishing, kelp, or peat to support themselves.

It was a very hard life. But Lewis MacAskill, whom the viewer is soon introduced to, doesn’t see it that way. He is one of just over a thousand residents of Assynt, who chose to stay and continue the crofting tradition.

“I regard the croft as an extension of who I am as a person,” MacAskill explains.

The small community of Assynt. Photo: Screenshot

MacAskill introduces us to some of the other members of the community. Anna is a sheepdog owner and trainer, whom we see herding sheep using the same techniques people here have used for centuries. Stuart is a passionate fisherman, who shares his love of Assynt’s natural landscape with his young son.

We also meet some of the creatives who have, MacAskill says, been drawn by the unique landscape and material culture. We see a potter using local materials, a fiddler, and a spinner on her spinning wheel.

The spinning wheel came to Europe from the Middle East by the 13th century, and was widely adopted by the 18th century, replacing the older drop spindle and distaff. Photo: Screenshot

MacAskill moved to the croft a decade ago, and doesn’t regret it. Having grown up visiting every summer, he has always felt drawn to the land and knows others feel the same. But a small, isolated community like Assynt is constantly in danger of depopulation. MacAskill hopes that people keep choosing to move back and stay, heeding the same call he did.

The film ends on this note, with a montage of scenes from life in Assynt and the landscape it sits in, while an elderly crofter sings a traditional Scottish song of homecoming.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8644. Florida Man Finishes Four Corners Walk Across America

After over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk. His route took him from coast to coast, then corner to corner, starting in Florida and ending in Maine, where a crowd of supporters met him last week.

Kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida. After struggling with drug addiction, mental illness, and the justice system during his early adulthood, he decided to become an endurance athlete and mental health advocate. On January 1, 2022, he began his walking project from the beach in Jacksonville.

Over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific. His plans expanded, and he undertook the challenge of walking to all four corners of the contiguous United States. From Long Beach, he headed to the northwesternmost point, Cape Flattery, also in Washington. After trekking south to San Diego, the next corner he headed for was all the way back in Florida, the southeast extremity.

Along the way, Edwards posted frequently on social media about his journey and his recovery from mental illness.

On October 25, Edwards reached West Quoddy Head Lighthouse in Lubec, Maine. This is the northeast corner of the U.S., and the finish line for Edwards. He walked a total of 19,544 kilometers in 1,022 days, averaging nearly 20km per day.

Edwards and supporters at the finish line. Photo: Kyndal Ray Edwards

A cross-country walking journey, Edwards says, has been his dream since 2013. But with the end of his Walking Across America project, Edwards is already ruminating on future challenges. Online, he has proposed going on an adventure with a stranger in all 50 states, running more ultra marathons, and undertaking endurance challenges on every continent. However, he has yet to commit to one.

The end of Kyndal Ray Edwards’s journey came only days before Karl Bushby, another long-distance trekker, completed his 28-year Goliath Expedition. The pair also happen, Edwards pointed out, to share a birthday.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8642. The Long Rainy Road

I have had extraordinary luck to largely avoid precipitation for many weeks. That is about to change.

Any hope of escaping with a dry tent vanished in the early morning hours. The first domino to fall. Now I had to hope that it wouldn’t be actively raining when it comes time to pack up camp. It quickly becomes impossible to keep my pack dry in such a scenario, how do I keep the pack dry when I have to disassemble and roll up my only dry place? Lucky for me, when light first broke the rain noise had stopped. I patted the walls of my tent to dispel some of the leftover water and checked the time. 6:17AM. I decided to save breakfast for later and go straight into packing up so I could check the sunrise and then get to hiking before the precipitation inevitably arrived. At The Pinnacle my instincts were correct, nothing but a small patch of orange glow that could have been a candy wrapper blowing in the wind. I was unbothered, any day where there is rain but I don’t have to pack up in the rain is alright with me. With rain imminent I chose to throw on my poncho, though that decision was partially based on the chillier than expected morning and early start time.

A little drizzle began to fall intermittently as I made my way along the rocky trail back to Pulpit Rock. Conveniently, I can save a few rocky steps by taking the clear driveway past the the Lehigh Valley Amateur Astronomical Society observatories. Its worth mentioning that the society provides a privy and trash can that can be used by hikers. They do ask that hikers don’t camp on the property or use flashlights, for obvious reasons. At the far end of the site I arrived at Pulpit Rock, which still offered a nice view despite the cloudy skies.

From there I didn’t hesitate to use the road down from the observatories all the way down to the Windsor Furnace Shelter. I had a quick breakfast and got back on trail before 8:30AM. Hardly any rain had fallen, I wondered if I’d again be getting lucky with the weather and get all the way back to my van without getting soaked. I pushed hard to get the 5 or so miles to Port Clinton done. I knew the steep leafy trail awaited me and I was holding my breathe to get through that section before any heavy rain arrived – it would not be fun going up that section if the trail was steep, leafy, and turning into a stream all at the same time.

Remarkably, the rain continued to hold off. I got closer and closer to Port Clinton, slowly realizing that the 60% chance of rain I saw for nearly every hour the day was landing in the 40% zone at least to start the day. I made it down the trail into town, back across the Schuykill River, and through the train yard. I charged up the hill, still expecting rain at any moment. The climb up proved tough, but not as treacherous as the climb down. This is the one time working against gravity actually works with you. Soon I was back on the ridge and heading toward the gravel road that would take me all the way back to my van on route 183. I thought that if the rain fell there it wouldn’t be a big deal, the hiking would at least be easy.

The Lehigh Valley Amateur Astronomical Society observatories near Pulpit Rock.

Breakfast at the Windsor Furnace Shelter.

A steep climb coming out of the Windsor Furnace Shelter.

I was just starting to think of the impossible. Could I get all the way back to my van without any serious rain? It would take about 3 and half hours to get all the way back to my van hiking at full bore on the gravel road. I didn’t have any stops to make, I was in a straight race with nature. My hopes slowly grew and then, with a single sound, were completely erased. On a downhill section of the road I heard thunder ahead. The forecast didn’t say anything about thunderstorms, but I suppose it didn’t say it would be dry for the better part of the morning either. I was fairly exposed on the road, there was going to be rain, and soon it came. I pulled my poncho back over me, I had stashed it over my shoulders during the climb to stay cool, staying dry was the priority now.

The wind blew and the rain progressed quickly from light drizzle to a steady downpour. The thunder bellowed louder and I began seeing flashes of lightning. The the rain started to feel sharp on my exposed hands. My gloves aren’t waterproof so it isn’t really worth it wear them in the rain. The rain had become freezing rain. Then it became hail the size of Nerds candy. The hail only lasted a few minutes, but the rain continued on. Although the day was in the mid 40s, the rain was ice cold. As soon as the rain became heavy my shoes and socks flooded. All I could do was shake my head and laugh, I had finally run out of luck, and things were regressing to the mean, emphasis on mean.

None of the surprisingly severe weather slowed me down. I was determined to get back to my van and get dry. The rain continued for almost 2 hours. When it did finally stop, I noticed that the water drops on the trees appeared frozen in place. It looked like ice hanging on the branches and made it look a lot like I was hiking on a rainy, cold winter afternoon. For good, measure, the sun decided to come out with about 30 minutes left. A nice thought, but it was going to take more than a few rays of sunlight to dry out my shoes.

Walking the gravel road just before the weather arrived.

Walking the gravel road just before the weather arrived.

It’s hard to see in the picture, but the scene had gotten considerably more wintery.

Near the end of the hike, the sun comes out.

#8639. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock. Her fiancé then lost his footing while trying to reach her.

A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair. Using ropes, slings, carabiners, and climbing harnesses, the group formed a human chain to reach both stranded hikers and pull them to safety.

The Electric Arms Race Has Gone Too Far: Tim Shuff questions the growing use of electric motors in outdoor adventure. He argues that the speed and convenience they create undermine traditionally self-propelled activities like paddling and cycling. Today, you can even buy battery-powered SUPs.

While recognizing that electric assistance can make outdoor sports more accessible, he thinks that its wider use will change wilderness areas, reshape trails, and create pressure to build increasingly powerful equipment.

Jan Spicka descends from Huascarán Sur. Photo: Matej Zak

A Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain: Climbing Peru’s Huascarán Sur turned into a tragedy for a group of five friends last July. Czech alpinist Jan Spicka describes how he and partner Matej Zak reached the 6,768m summit before he plunged into a hidden crevasse on the descent.

Matej’s quick reactions saved his life, but their three friends, Saul Mendoza, Chicho Ugarte, and Arti Salas, disappeared while attempting to descend by a different route. With no official mountain rescue in Peru, friends and volunteers pitched in. After 24 hours in the freezing conditions, they knew it was unlikely they would see their friends again. GPS tracks and later searches suggest they had fallen through a collapsing snow bridge.

He Felt Stuck in New York. So He Started Walking to California: Feeling trapped by unemployment and a lack of opportunities in New York, 29-year-old Chantz Rivera began walking across America. He set off with a tent, sleeping bag, and some supplies in a shopping cart. Over 149 days, he walked to California, pushing his cart 32 to 40km a day along highways and through small towns, documenting his progress for his growing number of online followers.

This Mountain Race Makes Runners Carry 60kg of Beer and Supplies Uphill: Slovakia’s annual Sherpa Rallye is one of the world’s unique mountain races. Competitors have to haul heavy loads of supplies up a 5.7km rocky trail to a remote hut in the High Tatras, nearly 2,000m above sea level.

Men carry 60kg, including a 30-liter keg of beer, while women carry 20kg, with the loads secured to wooden frames. The race was started in 1985 by mountain porter Viktor Beranek. The event brings together the region’s nosiči (traditional mountain porters) and also helps stock the remote hut ahead of winter.

A Hiker Slid Hundreds of Meters Down Mount Timpanogos: A female hiker was seriously injured after slipping off the trail near the summit of Mount Timpanogos in Utah. She slid several hundred feet down the steep mountainside before landing on a narrow cliff ledge. Newly released helicopter footage shows her being hoisted to safety. She was taken to hospital and is reportedly recovering.

We Need to Move Past the ‘Shut Up and Die Like a Man’ Mentality in the Mountains: Climber and paraglider Will Gadd reflects on the psychological impact of mountain accidents. Climbing culture often glorifies the dangers people face in the mountains while discouraging them from admitting they are struggling.

Gadd discusses the deaths of two close friends and challenges the underlying expectation that climbers should simply suck it up and carry on. After decades in the mountains, he has seen that the consequences of an accident extend far beyond the immediate incident, affecting survivors and their families and friends for years.

Two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia: Two hikers, identified as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter Selah Reed, have died in a suspected grizzly attack near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, British Columbia. Their bodies were found during a search after the pair were reported missing by their family.

This comes just a year after a separate grizzly attack in the same area severely injured four people, including three children. The trail remains closed as authorities continue their investigation.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8637. Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

Here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27. There will be more, as a few still scramble to raise the money or choose to keep their plans to themselves until the last minute. Because of the long charter flights, an expedition to Antarctica, even a “tourist” Last Degree trip, costs close to $100,000 — more, if you want to do something unusual. These are the journeys announced so far. Skiers hit the ice later this month.

Hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers. Skiers need to travel around 1,130km, averaging around 20km per day.

Brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole. Lumb previously completed a crossing of Norway’s Finnmarksvidda with guiding company Ousland Colliard.

Indian Neeraj Choudhary also trained with Ousland Colliard, crossing the Greenland Ice Sheet in 2024. He hopes to become the second Indian to ski solo and unsupported to the South Pole, following Satish Gogineni, who became the first in 2024-2025.

Satish Gogineni at the South Pole in 2025. Photo: Satish Gogineni

American Lucas Czarnecki will also ski solo and unsupported and claims he will livestream every moment of his journey: “What sets South Signal [his expedition name] apart from other polar expeditions is my commitment to bringing you along for every moment of this extreme adventure. Each day, I will be live-streaming my experience directly from the ice, sharing the raw reality of life on the polar plateau.”

Another American, Meghan Buchanan, will also tackle the route. She plans to start early, leaving for Antarctica on November 12.

Finally, German Dirk Langer will also attempt the route unsupported.

A Berkner Island start means a few extra kilometers, with skiers required to cover around 1,400km to the South Pole.

Max Worsley of the UK and Martin Nesse of Norway also plan to start in early November, but from the edge of Berkner Island. Max is the son of Henry Worsley, who died following an Antarctic expedition in 2015-2016. Max intends to follow much of his father’s final route.

At least two expeditions will begin at the Messner start, 911km from the South Pole. James Garnett of the UK and Norwegian Marius Rehn will each ski solo and unsupported.

Satish Gogineni will be back in Antarctica this year, hoping to build upon his Hercules Inlet experience. Gogineni’s 2026 plan is more ambitious: a solo, 2,000km journey from the outer edge of the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf to the inner edge of the Ross Ice Shelf via the South Pole. Gogineni is billing this as a “world-first human achievement” and the “longest solo traverse ever completed on the Antarctic continent.”

If successful, his route would indeed be longer than the truncated crossings of Colin O’Brady and Lou Rudd in 2018. However, his distance would still be well short of Borge Ousland’s 1997 expedition. Ousland became the first person to cross Antarctica solo and unsupported, though he occasionally used a rudimentary handheld kite known as a ski sail. Ousland skied for 65 days and covered 2,845km. At the time, sails were not considered “support.”

Last year, O’Brady tried a significantly longer expedition than his 2018 effort, attempting to ski from the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf to the tip of Berkner Island on the edge of the Ronne Ice Shelf, a total distance of over 2,800km. He eventually ended his crossing attempt after 100 days, with roughly 40% of his total distance remaining.

A map by PECS (the Polar Expeditions Classification Scheme) showing previous solo Antarctic crossing routes. Photo: PECS

Gogineni’s main challenge might be the weight of his sled. With so much weight spread over two sleds, O’Brady was forced to double carry in soft snow on the Ross Ice Shelf last year. A double carry involved shuttling half of his gear forward, then returning to pick up the rest. This meant he had to cover 15km for every 5km of progress. Gogineni says his sled will weigh 181kg.

Mardi Philips, Ida Olsson, and Nia Owens are calling themselves the Antarctic Valkyries and aim to become the “first all-female team to reach the South Pole of Inaccessibility.” They will start at Thorshammer Station (a spot near the Russian Novolazarevskaya Station in Queen Maud Land) and plan to kite-ski 2,500km, first aiming for the Pole of Inaccessibility (the middle of the Antarctic continent), and then continuing to their finish point at the South Pole.

The Antarctic Valkyries proposed route. Photo: Antarctic Valkyries

A Spanish scientific expedition will cross Antarctica by a new route in a unique wind-powered vehicle.

Part of the wind-sled involves a series of tents. Photo: La Vanguardia

Their “wind-sled ” is 15m long and consists of four modules. It is propelled using 20 kites of various sizes. The largest kite measures 150m² and the smallest 5m². The four-man team plans a 3,400km, 85-day journey from near Novolazarevskaya Station to the Italian research station Concordia, known as Dome C, on the Antarctic Plateau.

The wind-sled team’s proposed route. The green return route is planned for a future expedition. Photo: La Vanguardia

Meanwhile, three Argentine kayakers are preparing to paddle roughly 900km along the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula, from Argentina’s Esperanza Base to San Martín Base. Diego Linares, Juan Tomaselli, and Javier Siede will start their journey in January and plan to spend 30 to 40 days on the water.

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8634. Jetboil TrailCook 2.0L Stove Review: The Ultimate Stove for Group Backpacking Trips

Over the years, my backcountry cook setup has run the gamut from no-cook options to cooking for 12+ people on multiday treks across the Sierra Nevada or Grand Canyon.

On solo thru-hikes like the Pacific Crest Trail and Colorado Trail, I have historically used my trusted BRS stove to get the job done. And by job I usually just mean boiling water or, if I’m lucky during resupply, “cooking” tortellini. However, now as a backcountry guide I find myself cooking for other people much more often than just myself.

Cooking as a guide involves much more than boiling a pot of water to rehydrate a meal. Instead of ramen or Knorr sides, we are cooking things like egg sandwiches for breakfast, quesadillas with cilantro salsa for lunch, and backcountry fried teriyaki tofu with mixed veggies for dinner. So with all due respect to my original system, the BRS is not going to cut it out there when I’m trying to fry eggs or crisp up the edges of tofu.

These meals might sound elaborate, but they’re quite simple in the backcountry as long as you have the proper tools: I tested the Jetboil TrailCook 2.0L stove system this summer to see if it could get the job done.

Jetboil has really outdone itself with this one. Highlights include a do-it-all pot that’s large enough to feed the whole group, light enough to carry on the trail, and built with much of the same technology Jetboil users already know and love, plus key improvements over past models.

Straining boiling water into a larger pot while cooking for a large group on the Lost Coast Trail. The TrailCook 2.0L would soon after be used to soft boil some eggs.

MSRP: $199 Weight: 1 lb 6.24 oz or 630 g Dimensions: 17.3 cm x 14.5 cm Boil time:130 sec/0.5 liter water Capacity: 2 liters

While I think the Trailcook is one of the best all-in-one cook systems available on the market today, there is a specific use case for this setup. This system is overkill for a solo thru-hiker, but it really shines when you are cooking for more than two people on a backcountry outing. If your idea of camp cooking goes beyond boiling water and into preparing actual meals for you and your friends in the woods, the TrailCook 2.0L is definitely worth a look.

I took the TrailCook 2.0L system out on several outings during my initial testing period, putting it to work in a variety of group settings. It fed me and my coworkers during a three-day training trip on the Tahoe Rim Trail, helped cook for 18 students over six days in the Gila Wilderness, and performed beautifully while preparing meals for 11 women on the Lost Coast Trail.

Across each of these trips, the TrailCook 2.0L consistently felt like it was the right tool for the job. It never felt bulky or difficult to pack, yet it always had enough capacity to handle the demands of group cooking. What started as a product to test has quickly become an integral part of my kitchen setup on group trips, and I plan to continue taking it into the backcountry long after this review is published.

Boiling water rapidly while students participate in a field lesson before dinner.

FluxRing: This heat-transfer technology is one reason Jetboil stoves are among the best at heating quickly and efficiently.

Handling tabs and strainer: These user-friendly features let you drain the pot without burning your fingers on the hot lid. Hole for more exact pours on one side of the lid and strainer lines on the other.

Handling tabs and lid-lifter protected from heat.

Integrated 6,000 BTU/hr Burner: Powerful and effective. Just 130 seconds to boil half a liter of water.

Folding lockout silicone handles: Super handy for when the pot is full of heavy water or food. There is nothing worse than having to guess if your pot handle is going to hold.

Easy-ignite: The Trailcook lights just like a gas stove at home. The igniter felt intuitive and worked every time I used it. Keeping my fingers crossed it continues to do so.

Igniter with precision heat control features.

Precision heat control: This was a great feature for simmering or otherwise controlling the stove’s heat level! I haven’t seen this in the previous Jetboil versions I have owned, and I definitely suggest choosing a model with this feature included.

Compatible with accessories: While I didn’t test the stove with any accessories, the Summit Skillet will also fit with this system, as will the 1.5L cookpot, giving you multiple cooking surface options.

All-in-one packing: It’s so important to have gear that fits well into your pack. Despite this stove system’s large capacity, it’s so compact and easy to fit neatly into a backpack. The burner goes into a small bag, which can fit inside the pot along with a small (4 oz) fuel canister. The lid can then be put on and the handles folded to keep everything neatly packed together.

Stove with igniter and fuel all neatly held inside pot with handles keeping everything together. Hand shown for scale.

2Lpot: The size of this pot makes it ideal for large-group cooking, such as on my guided backcountry trips. While a second or third pot might be needed depending on group size, this system always boils water the quickest and gets the cooking off to a quick and easy start.

There are a lot of stoves on the market, but what makes a Jetboil a Jetboil is how quickly it can take water from snowmelt to a rolling boil. It has an insanely fast boil time, and that has undoubtedly contributed to Jetboil’s popularity over the years. When you’re cold, hungry, and ready for dinner, those extra few minutes start to matter.

The TrailCook 2.0L is designed for group cooking, and where it really stands out is in its combination of speed, efficiency, and packability. There are plenty of ways to cook for a group in the backcountry. For years, my setup was an MSR WhisperLite, a fuel bottle, and a large pot. That system works, but it also means carrying multiple pieces of gear, finding room for all of them in your pack, and waiting longer for water to boil.

The TrailCook 2.0L simplifies all of that. Everything nests neatly together, and thanks to Jetboil’s FluxRing technology, it boils water and cooks food much faster and more efficiently than the WhisperLite setups I’ve used in the past. It’s also not limited to just boiling water. The improved heat control makes it much easier to simmer, sauté, and cook actual meals instead of simply rehydrating food.

Soft-boiling eggs for the group. 6-minute boil followed by rapid cold dunk. Enjoy!

What impressed me most was how much cooking capacity Jetboil packed into such a compact system. A two-liter pot capable of feeding a group could easily feel bulky or awkward to carry, but I never felt like the TrailCook took up an unreasonable amount of pack space. On trips where I was cooking for anywhere from a handful of coworkers to nearly twenty students, I was consistently glad to have it along.

And while the TrailCook is certainly designed with the backcountry in mind, I think it deserves some credit for front-country camping too. If you’re cooking for two to four people, it offers a much more compact and portable alternative to hauling around a traditional Coleman stove and camp kitchen setup. You give up some cooking surface area, but you gain a lot in ease of use, packability, and speed.

I love knowing that when I get to camp after a long day of hiking or driving, my cook system is together in one place and takes just seconds to get going when it’s time to start dinner.

There are so many features on the TrailCook 2.0L that I love. Below is my love note to each of them:

Locking handles: Glorious. They lock out and feel sturdy and secure while cooking, and I never worried about them folding unexpectedly while moving a pot full of food around camp. A real blessing.

Lid: A design I found myself appreciating over and over again. Having both a pour hole and a built-in strainer makes draining pasta, pouring hot water, or straining veggies incredibly easy. It’s one of those simple features that feels like it was added after years of field testing and experience. It just makes sense.

Strainer side of lid, letting the water out while keeping the yum yum in.

No boil-over: If you’ve ever stood over a stove trying to prevent starchy pasta water from dumping all over your cook setup, you’ll understand why this is such a win. Even when I filled the pot well above the fill line, the contents didn’t bubble out like they did with some older Jetboil models.

Heat pads: The heat pads built into the lid sound minor, but they’re such a quality-of-life improvement. In the past, dumping water out of the lid usually meant grabbing a buff, a shirt sleeve, or whatever happened to be nearby to avoid burning my fingers on the hot metal. With the TrailCook 2.0L, this is a non-issue thanks to the little orange heat pads.

Speed: This thing is FAST. Jetboil has built its reputation on rapid boil times, and the TrailCook 2.0L is no exception. Whether I was melting snow, boiling water for a meal, or trying to get dinner on the table for a large group, I was consistently impressed by how quickly it got the job done. It worked so well that I could boil multiple pots of water on the Jetboil before the first pot finished boiling on my Whisperlite when I had both stoves going at once.

Capacity: It was large enough to comfortably cook for groups — including one trip where I was feeding 20 people — without ever feeling excessively bulky in my pack. That’s a tough balance to strike, and this system nailed it.

Built-in igniter: Backpacking stoves have come with built-in igniters for years, including Jetboils, but they’re often unreliable and break easily. In contrast, this one worked reliably throughout my testing. When everyone is hungry and waiting for dinner, being able to fire up the stove with the turn of a switch is a beautiful thing. Goodbye, “which pocket is my lighter in again?”

Heating rapidly is what Jetboil does best.

Pot support system: If I had one criticism of the TrailCook 2.0L, it would be the pot support system. I like the concept of the redesigned support arms and appreciate that the pot can be easily lifted on and off the stove. However, Jetboil markets the system as “self-centering,” and that wasn’t my experience.

I often found it surprisingly difficult to tell whether the pot was properly seated on the support arms. The grooves on the bottom of the pot are supposed to align with the arms on the stove, but there isn’t much tactile or visual feedback to let you know when everything is lined up correctly. More than once, I found myself double-checking the alignment before feeling confident enough to start cooking.

That being said, once the pot is properly seated, it feels stable and secure. The issue is getting it there. If one of the support arms misses its groove, the pot can sit unevenly, creating the potential for a spill if you’re not paying attention. It’s not a dealbreaker, but it’s one area where I think the user experience could be improved. I would love some external indication that the arms are in the grooves.

Weight: Again, this system shines in a specific use case. For solo hikers, the 2L capacity and 24 oz weight penalty don’t make sense. This isn’t a knock on the stove itself, which is meant for group trips.

The stabilizing arms shown along with bottom pot ring that sits on top.

Is this stove system worth my $199? My simple answer is yes. It has an overwhelming amount of useful, streamlined features and does the job well every single time. If I were in the market for a large-capacity Jetboil system, the TrailCook 2.0L would have my dollar.

Overall, the value-to-spend here is wonderful, but whether it’s worth it to you depends a lot on your use case. Do you need a large-capacity Jetboil system? Would the TrailCook 1.2L be enough capacity for your cooking needs? Do you cook for groups in the backcountry or are you a solo thru-hiker? Let these questions help guide your purchasing decision.

Shop the Jetboil Trailcook 2.0L Stove System

So good even my dog loves it. DogBowl 2.0L?

#8632. A Risky Summit Push on Everest

It’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest. Andrey Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have set off for the summit without oxygen, hoping the weather will hold. They are completely alone on the mountain, and the push is full of risk.

Everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m. That was their highest point during their earlier venture in October.  In addition, the wind may rise dramatically on Thursday, Vitor Baia, a Portuguese high-altitude meteorologist, told ExplorersWeb.

“It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.

The question is exactly when the wind will increase, and whether the climbers will have enough time to summit and descend to a safer altitude.

“They have three days of weak wind, until Wednesday [November 11], but then the wind will increase sharply,” said Baia.

He says the best summit day will be Tuesday, with clear skies and weak winds. “Then they could use Wednesday to descend,” he added. “[That day will have] some clouds but still acceptable wind speeds.”

The situation will worsen remarkably on Thursday, when the wind will shift from the west to the northwest and increase dramatically to 50 kph at 8,000m and 60kph at the summit.

In addition, avalanche hazards are still high due to the large amounts of snow after the latest storm two weeks ago. Finally, as winter approaches, it’s getting colder every day, the climbers reported.

After their first trip up ended in a tactical retreat as the cyclone hit, they retreated to Kathmandu to recover from some health issues. Now they are fit again and ready for a second try. They returned to Base Camp last Thursday. Not surprisingly, they found it covered in a thick new layer of snow. Breaking trail, they sank at some points up to their waists, Vasiliev reported.

“Our high-altitude boots were in a cache two hours ahead of us, so we used duct tape to seal our pant cuffs to our trekking boots, trying to keep the snow out,” Kondrashkin reported. They eventually reached the cache and continued up in an exhausting 14-hour-long effort to a second cache (their Camp 1), where they had left their tent and sleeping bags.

They were near an avalanche-prone area and several snow slides swept nearby, prompting them to wait a day before continuing. Meanwhile, Shipilov showed signs of food poisoning. Kodrashkin recalls that Saturday morning started with the following conversation:

“Vitalya, how are you feeling? Are we heading up?”

That answer needs some clarification. A professional like Vitaly Viktorovich [Shipilov] really only has two modes: “We’re going” and “I’m dying.”

In fact, Shipilov had a fever and acute pain in the lower back, so the team headed down to their base in Lobuche. As this was going on, the snow had time to sluff off from the previously avalanche-prone area.

After just one night of rest, Vasiliev confirmed they were going up again. If all went according to plan, they will spend tonight back in their tent above the Lho La. Unfortunately, the climbers have not shared their tracker showing their current location and progress. On their previous trip up, they reached some 7,500m on Everest’s West Shoulder, near the beginning of the West Ridge and the potential detour to the Hornbein Couloir.

Everest’s North Face from the base of the West Ridge. Photo: Sergey Kondrashkin

#8628. Winners of the Banff Mountain Film Festival Announced

The annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta. There, a celebration of mountain culture recognizes the best outdoor films and books of the past year. The climax of the festival took place this past weekend, and the winners of the 51st annual Banff Mountain Film Competition have now been announced.

The Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown. In this short documentary, sound engineer Hank Lentfer records the sounds of nature around his Alaska home, while caring for his mother with dementia. As Lentfer documents the degradation of the natural world, we witness the slow loss of his mother. Drawing together these two threads, the film explores connection despite, and through, loss, using sound.

Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”

The film also won the Grand Jury Prize at the Tribeca Film Festival.

In addition to a grand prize, the festival honors films in several categories. The winning film in the Adventure category was The Navigator, a feature-length work from director Jordan Manley. The film follows Nainoa Thompson, who was the first Native Hawaiian in six centuries to make the journey from Hawaii to Tahiti in a traditional voyaging canoe. Now, almost five decades later, Thompson and his crew make the journey again, using only traditional navigation techniques.

The best film in the Mountain Culture category was Land of Canaan, produced and directed by Maggie Lemere. Lemere’s film follows a group of Palestinian olive farmers, who work to protect their ancient olive groves amid the destruction by Israel. The film “illuminated the vital relationship of courage, vision, hope, and traditional ecological knowledge,” juror Rose Bush said, “in service of the essential value of sovereignty via mountain culture.”

In the Environment category, director James Dawson’s winning comedic documentary Derek vs Derek follows two Devon farmers, both named Derek. One Derek is an ardent dairy farmer while his environmentalist neighbor begins rewilding his land. A feud naturally ensues.

The Arc’teryx-sponsored Best Climbing Film was Zindabad, directed by Tom Fish. Fish follows Pakistani climber Mueez Ud Din into the Karakoram, alongside his uncle Javed Ali and French climber Mathieu Maynadier. Ud Din explores a remote, unknown glacier system, while the film examines what it means to be a Pakistani climber among peaks long claimed by international outsiders.

Directed by Alexis Berg, the Mountain Sports winner, Roots, follows trail runner Ruth Croft as she examines her future as an elite ultra-trail runner after an injury. Roots is “about an inner journey of healing and acceptance, rooted in the essential joy of running outdoors,” explained juror David Arnaud.

The Snow Sports winner centers on American skier Jessie Diggins. Diggins is the most decorated American cross-country skier ever, but Threshold, directed by Torsten Brinkema, reveals the deep personal struggles behind that success. Juror Beki Henderson noted that “the jury particularly commends Jessie Diggins for her extraordinary courage and honesty in sharing her story.”

There were more mountain films this year than you can even imagine. With 610 film submissions and 83 finalists, it’s no wonder that there are still more category winners.

Best short film winner Hello, Beautiful follows climber Alannah Yip as she struggles with identity, training for the Olympics while enduring medical hair loss. Director Darcy Hennessey created a film which “reminds us that personal transformation does not always come from pushing harder,” juror Kerry Stauffer explained.

For best feature film, the competition announced Ceremony, directed and produced by Banchi Hanuse. The film tells the story of the disappearance of the ooligan, a small fish, from British Columbia’s Bella Coola River. Jurors praised the film’s use of watercolor animation, personal stories, and community broadcasts to explore the importance of a seemingly unimportant little fish.

Director Marco Tribelhorn’s 75 seconds won the Creative Excellence Award. The film documents free-skier Jacob Wester’s 75-second-long battle for survival while trapped in an avalanche.

“A compelling visual treatment brings to life an experience that is impossible to imagine,” said Kerry Stauffer.

Last but not least, the Audience Choice Award went to Only Music // Snake River. Director Justin Fountain’s documentary follows a band that ditches the tour bus for a journey down the Snake River, seeking connection with strangers.

Tickets for the international film festival are now available. We have also covered the recently announced Banff Mountain Book Award winners.

#8625. A 3,300Km Walk Across Japan in Winter

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”

Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

The first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

Despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

From there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

Along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram

This is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he says the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

Tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka plans to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

#8622. The Not So Spiritual Camino Variant

Today marked Stage 2 of the Variante Espiritual, which we decided to hike in reverse. After days of walking against the main flow of pilgrims, yesterday was the first time we had the trail mostly to ourselves—aside from the crowds packing onto the upriver boats.

I woke up early to enjoy the solitude of breakfast on the patio with front-row views of the water. Watching the sun light up the morning sky with a plate of boiled quail eggs and a couple of strong cups of espresso was a wonderfully peaceful start. Today was billed as one of the most scenic and spiritual sections of the entire Camino.

At 8:00 AM, we stepped out into a cold breeze blowing across the water. The sun was just over the horizon, casting warm rays across the long footbridge as we crossed a small inlet bay to hike along the coast.

After walking along the coast for a bit, the trail angled inland. Following a slight climb up to a small church, we made our first wrong turn of the day.

Once we realized we were off the official Camino, we decided to forge our own path using Google Maps rather than backtrack.

The route crossed a high bridge over a busy highway before diving into a peaceful forest. Climbing up, we looked back and were amazed to see how far away the coast already looked. We could see the bay, distant coastal cities, and mountains on the horizon—all after just an hour and a half of walking.

As we exited the trees, we stumbled upon a massive vineyard stretching out across the hills. Unfortunately, the winery wasn’t open for another 20 minutes, so we kept moving. Walking through endless fields of grapes was incredible, and skipping the wine stop turned out to be a blessing given what the trail had in store for us later.

Walking against the grain of the Camino created endless confusion for everyone we passed:

They became genuinely concerned for us, which we thought was endearing. Every time we ran into a local, we used a mix of butchered Spanish and sign language to explain we were hiking toward Porto. Other times, we just smiled, waved, and kept moving.

We were deep in the countryside, passing beautiful solid-stone homes with immaculate gardens and tiny backyard vineyards.

By mid-morning, we had already knocked out 9 miles in under three hours.

We spotted the only café we’d seen all morning, grabbed a coffee and black tea, and relaxed on the porch overlooking the river. With such a fast pace early on, we assumed the rest of the day would be a breeze. We were very wrong.

The path ran right alongside the river for the next mile. The water was teeming with huge, two-foot-long fish—an invasive species, I assumed, since the river was practically overflowing with them. As the shade disappeared, the heat began to rise quickly.

At the junction of two busy multilane highways, we tried crossing via an elevated pedestrian bridge. As we climbed, thick briers started crowding the walkway—a red flag I should have noticed sooner. Reaching the other side, I realized we were totally off-track. We backtracked over the highway and ended up at a massive roundabout packed with nonstop traffic. Fortunately, we spotted a pedestrian tunnel to get us safely across.

On the other side of the highway, we stopped at a small roadside restaurant. This was a crucial stop: there were no grocery stores, cafés, or towns along our next stretch of the route.

Before leaving, I refilled our water bottles from the bathroom sink, knowing we were heading into a dry, rural stretch.

The next 5.5 km section was advertised as a tranquil forest trail running along a bubbling river with numerous waterfalls, climbing gently up to the Mosteiro de Santa María da Armenteira.

Since we couldn’t get a room at the monastery, our plan was to split off the Camino early and head to our accommodation in the tiny village of Silva. Armed with Google Maps, I figured it would be an easy shortcut.

Hot, tired, and out of water, we took a brief breather in a shaded cove when a cool breeze finally offered a moment of relief.

After climbing along the creek for 5 km, we left the Camino to forge our own path to Silva.

What started as a narrow, paved road quickly turned into a steep, unpaved logging trail climbing straight up through the forest. On Google Maps, it looked like a legitimate road; in reality, it was an overgrown, barely used dirt track.

I started to question: were we climbing all this way just to hit a dead end and be forced to hike all the way back down?

Knockerz was melting, I was completely exhausted, and we were both soaked in sweat and desperately thirsty. I hit that dazed, survival-mode state where you just keep putting one foot in front of the other, hoping the hill ends soon.

We kept pushing up the incline until, suddenly, the dirt track broke through the trees and met a paved road leading right to our door. Google Maps had come through.

Our lodging was a small, unmanned albergue with eight rooms and a shared kitchen.

Upon arrival our first stop was to hydrate. We went straight into the shared kitchen and drank glass after glass of cold water.

Next stop was to shower. We each took showers with our clothes on to rinse the caked-on sweat and dirt off both our bodies and gear at the same time.

Laying in the bed we were glad this day was done.

#8620. First Ski Descent of Meru Central

Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya. The skiers are still surprised by how lucky they were.

Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

“Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote. “We figured there was only a 3-in-10 chance of skiing the southwest face of Meru.”

But when they got there, the mountain was, they added, “generous” with them.

The three-peaked Meru massif, located in the Gangotri Glacier region of the Garhwal Himalaya, lies between Shivling and Thalay Sagar. It has three peaks: 6,660m Meru South, 6,310m Meru Central, and 6,450m Meru North. The ski descent line is in purple. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein

“We spent six days of reconnaissance and three [days] climbing the peak, [thanks to] an unprecedented stroke of luck in finding a way through the icefall and perfect snow in the upper section,” she explained.

The icefall on Meru Central. Photo: Boris Langenstein

The icefall at the base of the peak was indeed one of the most complex passages. The pair climbed a 15m pitch of WI4 and left a safety rope, which they also used to rappel down after the ski descent, Duperier told PlanetMountain.

Otherwise, the pair of regular expedition and skiing partners climbed alpine-style and pretty fast, reaching the summit in less than eight hours. According to their research, they completed the second-ever ascent of the southwest face of Meru, after an Indian team in 2023.

At the summit on Meru Central. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein

The skiers estimate they covered 1,500m on their descent, with some sections reaching 50 °. Snow conditions were good overall, hard but with a good grip.

“We skied like little monkeys on the wires in Rishikesh,” Duperier posted on social media. “It was just incredible, truly beautiful!”

While the climbers rappelled down the icefall onto the glacier below, the ski descent itself had no rappels or interruptions.

Duperier barely had time to return home to France to pick up a Piolet d’Or for the first alpine-style ascent of the Schell Route on the Rupal Face of Nanga Parbat, followed by the first ski descent from the 8,125m summit.

Tiphaine Duperier at the Piolets d’Or ceremony. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

#8616. Arctic Town Kills Dozens of Grizzlies Feeding on Dump

For years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories

It was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

“They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” said Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”

Inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

“We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” said local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

Many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories

#8614. What If Money Wasn’t the Barrier to Your PCT Dream?

The Pacific Crest Trail is a dream for thousands of people. Spanning 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada, the trail offers the opportunity to step away from everyday life, immerse yourself in the outdoors, and experience something that can be difficult to put into words.

But getting to the trail takes more than a dream. For many aspiring thru-hikers, the financial commitment is one of the biggest barriers. Between gear, food, transportation, and the ability to step away from work for several months, the cost of a thru-hike can put the experience out of reach before someone even takes their first step.

The PCT Grant was created to help change that.

Through the Trail Angel Fund, the PCT Grant provides $5,000 annually to a Washingtonian (and so far this year, we have raised enough money to send off TWO hikers!) between the ages of 18 and 33 who dream of thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail. Its mission is to make long-distance hiking more accessible by easing the financial burden and giving someone the opportunity to pursue an experience they might not otherwise be able to afford.

At its heart, the program is about expanding access to the outdoors and recognizing that the transformative experiences found on trail shouldn’t be limited to those who can afford them.

2026 was the first year the PCT Grant came to life and chose its first recipient to take on thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail. That person was me! The face behind the screen: Cappy. Post trail, I have joined the PCT Grant Committee to spread some magic with hopes of creating that same opportunity for others.

Receiving the grant was a lifeline. It wasn’t just financial support; it was the difference between being able to pursue this dream and having to put it on hold. It gave me room to take a chance on myself and say yes to an experience that changed the way I see what’s possible in life.

As this year’s recipient, I experienced firsthand what this kind of support can make possible. The trail taught me a lot about the power of choice and trust. The power of choosing something before knowing exactly how it will unfold, doing it scared, and learning to become comfortable with the uncomfortable.

Spending five months on trail offered so much more than the physical accomplishment of a thru-hike. I discovered how much we are capable of when we give ourselves the opportunity to find out. This trail changed my life, and it will continue to do so.

As the program enters its second year, the focus is on growing awareness, strengthening community support, and building a foundation for future recipients.

Currently, the grant is funded to support one hiker annually, with a longer-term vision of expanding its reach and helping more aspiring thru-hikers access the trail. From our fundraising efforts (a post trail Q&A with Cappy and other media platforms helping to spread the word) we have raised enough money to fund a second hiker this coming year.

Donations play an important role in making that possible. Every contribution helps sustain the program and move it closer to supporting additional hikers in the years ahead. We want to continue to grow this program so that even more hikers can set foot on the trail.

Applications for the 2027 PCT Grant are open through January 31, 2027. If you’re a Washingtonian between 18 and 33 with a dream of hiking the PCT, this could be an opportunity to make it happen.

And for those who have already experienced the magic of the trail, consider helping someone else get there.
